analysis.one_liner: Raises the bar for the DEA to immediately suspend a drug distributor's registration for diversion.
analysis.headline: Passed both chambers without a single recorded opposing vote and became law on April 19, 2016.
analysis.plain_summary: This law changes how the DEA can police companies that ship prescription opioids. Before it, the DEA could immediately suspend a distributor's registration when it posed an 'imminent danger' to public safety. The law redefines 'imminent danger' to require a 'substantial likelihood of an immediate threat' of death or serious harm, and it requires a written notice, a 30-day appearance date, and a chance for the company to submit a corrective action plan before the DEA can revoke or suspend a registration. It also directs health agencies to report to Congress on obstacles to patient access and pain-management prescribing.
analysis.who_benefits: Drug distributors and manufacturers facing DEA enforcement actions get a clear, higher legal bar the agency must meet before freezing their registrations, plus a built-in opportunity to negotiate corrective action plans instead of losing their licenses. Supporters also argued it protects pain patients from overly aggressive enforcement cutting off legitimate medication access.

how_it_helps.text: Redefines 'imminent danger to the public health or safety' so an immediate suspension order requires a 'substantial likelihood of an immediate threat' of death, serious bodily harm, or abuse due to a registrant's failure to control diversion [S5].

Requires DEA orders to show cause to state the specific legal basis for denial, revocation, or suspension, set an appearance at least 30 days out, and notify the registrant it may submit a corrective action plan, which the Attorney General must then weigh before continuing [S5].

Directs FDA, SAMHSA, AHRQ, and CDC to report to Congress on obstacles to legitimate patient access, gaps in pain-management medical training, and enhancements to prescription drug monitoring programs [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If enforcement is slower, suspect shipments of prescription opioids keep flowing while cases are negotiated, and communities absorb the resulting addiction and overdose deaths. The record here shows the statutory mechanics, not the measured aftermath.

drawbacks.text: The new 'substantial likelihood of an immediate threat' standard is a higher bar than the DEA previously operated under, making immediate suspensions of distributors harder to obtain [S5].

The mandatory 30-day show-cause process and corrective-action-plan step give suspected violators time to keep shipping and negotiate their way out of suspension, even though immediate suspension orders are formally exempt from the new requirements [S5].

The required congressional report must consult drug manufacturers, wholesale distributors, pharmacies, and pharmacy benefit managers among its feedback sources, embedding the regulated industry in the government's assessment of diversion [S5].

The strongest good-faith objection supporters would raise: criminal prosecutions are unaffected, immediate suspensions remain available in extreme cases, and distributors had argued DEA acted on thin records; the bill adds due process, not an exemption [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The due-process protections for registrants and the pain-management education report are real, but the law's most consequential change cuts in the other direction: it raises the threshold and slows the machinery the DEA used to freeze distributors suspected of shipping diverted opioids, at the height of the opioid epidemic. That benefit to industry dwarfed the educational and reporting provisions in practical importance.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the Senate by unanimous consent on March 17, 2016, and the House passed it without objection on April 12, and the President signed it on April 19, 2016 [S7].

narrative.text: Introduced by Sen. Orrin Hatch in February 2015 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee [S1][S7].
The committee reported it favorably on February 11, 2016, without a written report, and placed it on the Senate calendar [S7].
The Senate passed it by unanimous consent on March 17, 2016 — no roll-call vote, no debate requiring one [S7].
Rep. Leonard Lance asked unanimous consent to take it up in the House, and it passed without objection on April 12, 2016 [S7].
The President signed it on April 19, 2016; it became Public Law 114-145 [S4][S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The major drug distributors came out ahead. The law gave them a higher bar and a negotiation window against DEA license suspensions, and widely reported investigations later found DEA immediate-suspension actions against the big distributors slowed dramatically during the opioid crisis. No member of Congress is on record opposing it.

for.name: Tom Marino
for.role: U.S. Representative (PA), sponsor of the House companion H.R. 471

for.name: Healthcare Distribution Alliance and its major members
for.what_they_did: Lobbied for the measure; widely reported that the industry pushed the bill to rein in DEA immediate suspensions.

for.name: Leonard Lance

for.name: Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: Signed the bill into law on April 19, 2016.

against.name: Joseph Rannazzisi
against.role: Former head of DEA's Office of Diversion Control
against.what_they_did: Publicly warned the law was written to favor distributors and would cripple DEA's ability to immediately suspend suspect registrants.

against.name: DEA enforcement officials
against.what_they_did: Per widely reported accounts, opposed earlier versions and lost a two-year effort to block the bill; no member of Congress voted against the final version.

sides.party_line_note: There were no roll-call votes and no recorded objections: the Senate passed it by unanimous consent with 1 Democratic and 3 Republican cosponsors, and the House passed it without objection [S6][S7].

industries.industry: Wholesale drug distributors (McKesson, Cardinal Health, AmerisourceBergen)
industries.note: The law raises the threshold for immediately suspending a distributor's registration and adds a 30-day show-cause and corrective-action-plan process before revocation or suspension. Widely reported investigations later found DEA immediate suspensions against the largest distributors effectively stopped after enactment.

Manufacturers face the same registration, suspension, and revocation process as distributors, so the higher bar and mandatory corrective-action window protect them too. The law also requires the government's diversion report to consult with manufacturers.
They benefit from reduced risk of registration suspension and from the report's attention to patient access, but also bear diversion-control obligations.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and health insurers
industries.note: They are listed as consultees for the required congressional report, gaining a formal seat in shaping opioid policy recommendations.
